evidence.claim: The Quiver documentation Limits page is marked 'Last updated: 2024-06-03 (applies to Quiver 2.x)' and lists 100,000,000 vectors per collection, 4,096 dimensions and 64 metadata fields per vector.
evidence.applicability: This is where the engineer's 100M-cap claim comes from. The page says it covers Quiver 2.x only.
evidence.limitations: The page is more than two years older than Quiver 3.x. No current (3.x) limits page was supplied or found.

evidence.claim: The Quiver changelog entry for 3.0.0 (2026-02-02) says: 'Per-collection limit raised to 1,000,000,000 vectors (sharded collections).'
evidence.applicability: This supersedes the 2.x 100M limit for Quiver 3.0 and later. 300M sits inside the stated 1B limit, so the 100M-cap premise looks out of date.
evidence.limitations: The entry is one line. It does not say whether filters, recall and latency behave the same on sharded collections, how shards are configured, or whether sharding is automatic. The sources say nothing about cross-shard caveats.

evidence.claim: The Quiver changelog entry for 3.0.0 (2026-02-02) adds a 'New filtered-HNSW index: metadata filters applied during graph traversal instead of post-filtering.' The 2.1.0 entry (2024-04-30) describes 'Metadata filtering (post-filter).'
evidence.applicability: Quiver 2.1 used post-filtering and 3.0 moved to in-traversal filtering. This changes filtered-query performance a lot, so benchmarks of 2.1 do not describe current Quiver.
evidence.limitations: The changelog does not quantify the performance gain.

evidence.claim: The Quiver changelog entry for 3.2.0 (2026-07-14) says: 'Private/VPC deployment via Helm chart is GA.'
evidence.applicability: Quiver supports self-hosted VPC deployment, but it has been GA for only about 4 months as of 2026-11-11.
evidence.limitations: The entry gives no details on HA, replication, rolling upgrades, backup/restore or observability. The changelog shows no release after 3.2.0, and its completeness is unknown.

evidence.claim: Tessellate Inc. published a benchmark dated 2026-05 on 50M vectors, 768-dim, with a 10% selectivity filter. It reports filtered p95 of 34 ms for Tessellate 4.0 and 141 ms for Quiver 2.1, and concludes 'Tessellate is over 4x faster for filtered search.'

source.title: Tessellate vs. Quiver: filtered vector search

evidence.applicability: This is the source of the engineer's 4x claim. The stated figures give 141/34 ≈ 4.15, so the 'over 4x' arithmetic matches the table. But it compares Tessellate with Quiver 2.1 (post-filter), and the benchmark is dated 2026-05, about 3 months after Quiver 3.0 shipped filtered-HNSW (2026-02-02).
evidence.limitations: The vendor ran it on its own product. It tested an outdated Quiver version at 50M scale (one-sixth of the target). It reports no recall, QPS, hardware or tuning details, and no reproducible configs. Its methodology cannot be checked.

verification.method: Read the supplied fixture; ratio checked against table values

evidence.claim: OpenANN-Bench 2026-09 describes itself as a 'community benchmark, reproducible configs published'. It ran 200M vectors, 768-dim, a 10% selectivity filter, 400 QPS, on 3-node clusters of identical hardware. Tessellate 4.0 scored filtered p95 31 ms at Recall@10 0.95. Quiver 3.1 scored filtered p95 38 ms at Recall@10 0.97. The page notes it was 'Not tested above 200M vectors. Results depend heavily on filter selectivity.'
evidence.applicability: This is the most relevant evidence. On current Quiver, both engines meet p95 < 50 ms at 400 QPS. Tessellate is about 1.2x faster (38/31), while Quiver has higher recall (0.97 vs 0.95). That contradicts the 4x claim for current versions.
evidence.limitations: Recall differs between the engines, so the latency numbers are not at the same recall. It used 200M vectors rather than 300M and a single selectivity of 10%. It does not specify hardware, tuning or memory footprint. Its claims of independence and reproducibility could not be checked externally (see E8).

evidence.claim: Web searches found no public documentation for a 'Quiver' vector database with sharded collections or 1B-vector support. The only projects named Quiver were unrelated small embedded libraries (PyPI quiver-vector-db, tfmv/quiver). Nothing was found for a 'Tessellate' vector database, including its licensing, Helm or self-hosted deployment.

source.title: Fast embedded vector database with Python bindings

evidence.applicability: The supplied documents are the only evidence on either product. Licensing, support, HA and cost for both engines cannot be established from public sources.
evidence.limitations: This is based on search snippets only, with no fetch. Absence from search results does not prove the products don't exist. They may be private, new or named differently.

evidence.claim: A web search for 'OpenANN-Bench' found no benchmark by that name. The closest matches were other filtered-ANN benchmarks (the arXiv 2602.11443 extended ANN-Benchmarks, arXiv 2509.07789, and Qdrant's filtered search benchmark).

source.title: Filtered Approximate Nearest Neighbor Search in Vector Databases: System Design and Performance Analysis

evidence.applicability: The independence and reproducibility of OpenANN-Bench (the planner's assumption) cannot be confirmed externally. The published configs were not located.
evidence.limitations: The fetch of arxiv.org failed (host not allowed in session), so this rests on search snippets only.

evidence.claim: Search snippets on filtered-ANN research say that filter selectivity strongly affects performance. One snippet reports that partition-based IVFFlat outperformed graph-based HNSW for low-selectivity queries (arXiv 2602.11443, Feb 2026). Qdrant's 'filterable HNSW' is described as a design for in-graph filtering.

source.title: Filtered Approximate Nearest Neighbor Search in Vector Databases

evidence.applicability: Supports testing several selectivities (1%, 10%, 50%) on the team's real filters, since 10%-only benchmarks may not carry over.
evidence.limitations: The general claim is supported by a snippet plus a fixture, and the specific IVF-vs-HNSW finding comes from a snippet only. None of it is specific to Quiver or Tessellate.

verification.method: Search snippet plus fixture statement 'Results depend heavily on filter selectivity'

evidence.claim: The user says the workload is 300M document embeddings of 768 dimensions with metadata filters, a p95 target under 50 ms at 400 QPS, self-hosted in a VPC. The user also says an engineer wants to drop Quiver because of a 100M cap and a 4x filtered-query slowdown.
evidence.applicability: Defines the requirements and the premises being tested.
evidence.limitations: The request gives no filter selectivity distribution, filter complexity, write rate, recall target or budget.

evidence.claim: No evidence was found on either engine's performance at 300M vectors, memory, disk or node footprint, quantization or on-disk index support, ingestion or upsert behaviour, licensing, or support options.
evidence.applicability: C5, C6 and C7, and C2 at 300M scale, cannot be scored from the evidence. A proof-of-concept and vendor inquiries are needed.
evidence.limitations: Neither the supplied sources nor the web searches covered these topics.

unresolvedGaps.reason: The changelog says sharded collections reach 1B, but no current Quiver 3.x limits doc or sharding documentation was available. Caveats on filters, cross-shard recall and latency are unknown.
No benchmark above 200M vectors or at selectivities other than 10% was found. A proof-of-concept at 300M with real filters at 400 QPS and fixed recall is required.
The team's filter selectivity distribution and complexity are not provided. Tessellate's metadata-field limit is not documented in the sources.
Neither source covers HA, replication, upgrade or backup details for either engine. No Tessellate self-hosted documentation was found on the web.
No memory, storage or quantization data for either engine.
No ingestion or concurrent-write behaviour data for either engine.
No licensing or support information was found for either engine. The products are not identifiable in public web search.

The recomputed ratio is 141/34 ≈ 4.15 and is confirmed from the table. But the Tessellate benchmark's hardware, QPS, recall and tuning are not disclosed, so its methodology cannot be audited. OpenANN-Bench independence could not be verified: no external page was found, and the arxiv.org fetch was blocked by the session network policy.
Could not confirm whether Quiver 3.2 regresses against 3.1 or whether Tessellate has a release newer than 4.0. No vendor release notes were found beyond the supplied Quiver changelog.
